What is the Ministry of Defence's official position on UFOs,

The Ministry of Defence's position on UFOs is simply that they look at sighting reports
with a view to assessing whether there's any evidence of a threat to the defence of the United Kingdom.
Now, they say that unless evidence of any threat is found,
they play no further part in an investigation and they're not under any
remit to find out what the object was. I suppose my own personal position is
somewhat akin to that but I perhaps take it a step further. It's my view that one
can not say for sure whether there's evidence of a threat until the point at
which you've satisfied yourself what the object was. So it's my view that okay
say, you know, we're not interested unless there's a threat, but let's be very clear
what something is before we write it off and say, oh, there's nothing to worry about.
Okay.

interesting aspects. They wrote their memoirs, they used official knowledge and experience

Well, the UFO investigations that I did for the Ministry of Defence

I've now been moved on to other duties, but because that is now my current job,

My three-year tour of duty in secretariat air staff simply ended when I came to the end of that posting.
In fact, I was promoted. There was nothing sinister about that. I was not fired.
I'm still at the Ministry of Defence, although on other duties.
And three years is actually pretty average for a tour of duty.
So there was nothing sinister, I was not moved on to get me out of the way.
I guess that you'd say that my conclusions at the end of that particular tour of duty were very much open.
I believe that I had found good data suggesting that there was something to the UFO phenomenon.
Certainly some things to suggest that there were decidedly unconventional,
possibly extraterrestrial causes to some of this.
That's not to say that I could prove it in a court of law.
It is very difficult studying UFOs because, as I've always said,
you are generally speaking studying something that is not there anymore.
Unlike most science where you've got something in the lab,
setting aside the view of the most vehement conspiracy theorists,

I did not have that.

I presented my findings to my Ministry of Defence bosses,

yes, I agree, that's fascinating.
Difficult to see what conventional explanation there could be.

I've got no way of saying for sure what happened after I presented some of my findings

What happened to the photographic evidence and the soil samples? Where did those go?
Things like photos and videos, when they're sent to the MOD, what you actually have to remember is that they are actually copyright to somebody else.
Most of the material we get simply comes to us from interested or concerned members of the public.
and most times that material is then returned to them on request.
There is no hidden archive, no treasure trove of secret films and videos in our basement.
That's not to say that we haven't kept a few things over the years,
but old film stock, for example, as I'm sure most people will know,
actually deteriorates fairly quickly.
So there was a lot of stock from the 50s, which, sad to say, is now gone forever.
Hmm.
If there was an incident in England, such as a sighting or landing of a UFO, who would deal with it and how?
Any UFO sighting that occurred in Britain, details of it should have been filtered to me at the Ministry of Defence so that I could launch an investigation.
Now the investigation that I launched very much depended on the quality of the data given to me.
If somebody said a few days ago I saw a vague light in the sky, frankly, there's very little I can do.
If somebody gives me an exact date, an exact time, I can do a lot more.
I can speak to the military, I can try and cross-reference the details and correlate it with some kind of scheduled activity.
I can speak to the Air Force, I can speak to the local police, I could get hold of radar tapes, for example.
I could even go out to the civilian UFO research groups and suggest that we exchange data.
So there were a lot of things that I could do.
Depending on...
Yeah. Now, as for there being any protocol for dealing with something that goes beyond that, landing for example,
the answer, sad to say, is no.
I have often said that I believe there should be a protocol.
as we say in Britain, certainly so far as the military are concerned,
we call it a standard operating procedure, an SOP.
Now, I believe that because of factors like the potential biological hazard
from any two-way contact between us and a civilization
that has evolved on another ecosystem, on another world,
I believe there are issues here, and I believe there should be such a procedure,
But to the best of my knowledge, sadly, there is as yet no such SOP.
Thank you. How many sightings would you say were reported to you during your three-year period at the MOD?
Each year I got somewhere between 200 and 300 UFO reports.

And of those, quite frankly, 90% after a reasonable investigation could be dismissed as nothing more exciting than a misidentification of something perfectly ordinary, whether it's aircraft lights, satellites, meteors, weather balloons, or the whole list of usual suspects.
So 10% of the 200?
Yes. So each year I'm estimating that somewhere around 20 or 30 good cases,
cases where even after a long, hard look at what was given to me,
I was able to say these are not explained, and what's more,
it's not simply a question of insufficient data.
It is some pretty good data, a report perhaps from a military witness,
between a civil aircraft and a UFO, something on radar, things like that.
20 or 30 good cases a year.

And that would certainly go into my category of good evidence to support something unusual,
possibly something extraterrestrial.
I've looked into the Bentwaters case, obviously not at the time.
years before my tour of duty. But I've looked retrospectively at the case, I've spoken to

out.
